paras: The White Cap threat against Joseph Crecelins took place in mid-April 1888, when a band of "White Caps" in southern Indiana called out an elderly lawyer accused of improper attentions to a young woman and ordered him to leave town. The accounts differ on the threat, which one brief described as lynching, a Louisville dispatch as tar and feathers, and a New Albany dispatch as half an hour to get out of town; all agree that he left. The papers reported it as one stop on a night raid in which the band also whipped three brothers and warned another man to leave, part of a spring of White Cap activity around New Albany.

In the spring of 1888 dispatches from New Albany described the White Caps of Crawford and Harrison counties as "regulators" who whipped or drove out people they accused of idleness, drunkenness or immorality. A dispatch printed in the Rock Island Argus said the organization was understood to be made up of reputable farmers and was determined to rid Crawford County of its "bad characters."

According to a New Albany dispatch printed in the New York Sun and the Washington Evening Star, a band of fifty-seven White Caps rode into the suburbs of New Albany on a Saturday night, took three sons of a widow named Jones from their beds, tied them to trees and whipped them. The band then warned William Wright "under pain of death" to leave Harrison County, although the dispatch called him "apparently a law-abiding citizen." From Wright's house the band went to Taswell, where a sixty-two-year-old lawyer from Leavenworth "who had been too demonstrative in his attentions to a young girl" was called out and given half an hour to leave town. He left without delay, and at one o'clock in the morning the White Caps were seen riding toward Birdseye.

A shorter Louisville dispatch placed the raid "in the country back of New Albany" and said the lawyer had been paying attention to Mrs. Jones's daughter. In that version the band threatened him with tar and feathers unless he left for home within half an hour, and he went at once. A brief in the Chicago Citizen, datelined New Albany, April 17, gave his name as Joseph Crecelins, a sixty-year-old lawyer living in Crawford County, and said he was "alleged to have been intimate with Miss McDaniel, aged 20."
The coverage contains no report of an arrest, charge or other official action concerning the lawyer, or of what became of him.

The raid reached readers in two wire versions: a Louisville dispatch ran on April 16 in the New-York Tribune and the St. Paul Daily Globe and on April 18 in the Indiana State Sentinel of Indianapolis. The New Albany dispatch appeared on April 16 in the Sun and on April 17 in the Evening Star, and the Shepherdstown Register in West Virginia reprinted it on April 20. The Chicago Citizen's brief of April 21, the only account to name the lawyer or the young woman, ran under the headline "Beginning Their Spring Campaign."

Headlines ranged from approval to alarm: the Globe titled its version "Good Work by White Caps," while the Star's headline said the band was becoming "more and more daring in their raids." Only the New Albany dispatch voiced doubt about one of the band's targets, noting that what Wright had done was not known; no paper questioned the charge against the lawyer, and none stated the race of anyone involved.

The Citizen also called the young woman Miss McDaniel and made the whipped men her brothers, punished "for getting drunk and not supporting their mother," whereas both wire versions identified the brothers as the sons of the widow Jones. The Louisville dispatch as printed in the Tribune and the Sentinel placed the raid on Friday night, April 13, while the Globe's version and the New Albany dispatch placed it on Saturday night, April 14. Because the Citizen's account matches the others on the warning to William Wright and on an elderly lawyer accused of attentions to a young woman, it appears to describe the same raid, though it is the only source for his name and gives his age as sixty rather than sixty-two.

reader.title: White Cap threat against Joseph Crecelins
bases: A band of White Caps riding at night called out a lawyer accused of improper attentions to a young woman and forced him to leave town under threat, during a raid that also whipped three men and warned another to leave (A3, A5, A9).

No one was killed: the lawyer was threatened (with lynching in A9, with tar and feathers in A3) and left town within half an hour (A3, A4), so the episode is a threat by a band acting as self-appointed regulators, not a completed lynching (A5).

Two independent wire versions (Louisville, A3/A6; New Albany, A4/A5) and the Citizen brief (A9) agree that White Caps forced an elderly lawyer accused of attentions to a young woman to leave town, though they differ on the threat, the woman's name and the date.

accounts.label: New Albany dispatch
accounts.gist: Fifty-seven White Caps whipped the widow Jones's three sons, warned William Wright out of Harrison County, then called out a 62-year-old Leavenworth lawyer at Taswell, 'too demonstrative' toward a young girl, and gave him half an hour to leave; he left without delay.

accounts.label: Louisville dispatch
accounts.gist: After whipping the Jones boys and warning Wright, the band threatened a Leavenworth lawyer who had paid attention to Mrs. Jones' daughter with tar and feathers unless he left for home within half an hour; he went at once.

accounts.label: Chicago Citizen brief
accounts.gist: Joseph Crecelins, a 60-year-old Crawford County lawyer alleged to have been intimate with Miss McDaniel, 20, was threatened with lynching; her brothers were whipped and Wright was visited.

framing.detail: The St. Paul Daily Globe headed the Louisville dispatch 'Good Work by White Caps.'
The Evening Star's 'More and More Daring in Their Raids' treated the band as a growing menace and doubted Wright's guilt, but reported the charge against the lawyer without comment.
The Citizen ran a short wire brief under 'Beginning Their Spring Campaign.'
The Rock Island Argus, covering the band's whippings later that week, called every Crawford County man it whipped 'a desperado' and its members reputable farmers.
